summary.text: Quadratic reciprocity makes 5 a square modulo such a prime; choosing a representative root \(x\) and setting \(n=x-1\) gives \(p\mid T(n)=(n+1)^2-5\), with the needed size and exceptional-index conditions (the case \(p=11\) is handled directly). A closed evaluation of the continued fraction gives the relevant rational as \(2(n-2)T(n)/((n-2)D)\); writing \(T(n)=pm\), size and factorial-divisibility arguments give \(m\mid(n-3)!\), while parity shows \(2m\mid D\) and a prime-factor argument shows \(p\nmid D\), so the fraction reduces to \(p/s\) and its required denominator is exactly \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}\qquad (2\le k<n-1),
\]
with terminal value
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)-\frac n{-4}=(n-1)+\frac n4.
\]
Thus the continued fraction in the definition of the sequence is
\[
C_n=\frac1{R_2(n)}.
\]
If the rational number \(R_2(n)\) is written in lowest terms as \(N/D\), with \(D>0\), then \(C_n=D/N\), and hence the reduced denominator of \(C_n\) is \(|N|\). We shall prove that for each prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\), one can choose \(n\) for which the reduced numerator of \(R_2(n)\) is exactly \(p\).

For \(n\ge3\), put
\[
T(n)=n^2+2n-4=(n+1)^2-5.
\]
We first derive an exact expression for \(R_2(n)\).

For integers \(\kappa\ge0\), define
\[
F_\kappa=F(n,\kappa)=\sum_{j=\kappa+3}^{n-1}(j-3)!
 =\sum_{i=0}^{n-\kappa-4}(i+\kappa)!,
\]
where an empty sum is understood to be zero. Also set
\[
G_\kappa=G(n,\kappa)=4(n-1)!+(n-2)T(n)F_\kappa.
\]
Whenever \(\kappa+4\le n\), separating the first term of the sum gives
\[
F_\kappa=\kappa!+F_{\kappa+1}.
\]
Applying this twice, and using \((\kappa+1)!=(\kappa+1)\kappa!\), gives, whenever \(\kappa+5\le n\),
\[
(\kappa+2)G_{\kappa+1}=(\kappa+1)G_\kappa+G_{\kappa+2}. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the contributions of the constant term \(4(n-1)!\) agree on both sides, and after dividing the remaining terms by \((n-2)T(n)\), the assertion is precisely the identity obtained from the two displayed recurrences for \(F\).

We claim that for \(0\le\kappa\le n-4\),
\[
R_{\kappa+3}(n)
 =\frac{(\kappa+3)(\kappa+1)G_\kappa}
 { (\kappa+2)G_{\kappa+1}}. \tag{2}
\]
This follows by downward induction from the end of the continued fraction. For the terminal case \(n=\kappa+4\), one has
\[
F_\kappa=\kappa!,\qquad F_{\kappa+1}=0.
\]
Substitution into the right side of (2), followed by use of
\((\kappa+3)!=(\kappa+3)(\kappa+2)(\kappa+1)\kappa!\), reduces it to
\[
\kappa+3+\frac{\kappa+4}{4},
\]
which is exactly \(R_{n-1}(n)\). More explicitly, in this case
\[
T(n)=(\kappa+2)(\kappa+8)+4,
\]
and the expression in (2) simplifies to
\[
\frac{4(\kappa+3)(\kappa+1)+T(n)}{4(\kappa+2)}
 =\frac{5\kappa+16}{4}
 =\kappa+3+\frac{\kappa+4}{4}.
\]

For the induction step, suppose the formula is known one level farther into the fraction. Then
\[
R_{\kappa+4}(n)
 =\frac{(\kappa+4)(\kappa+2)G_{\kappa+1}}
 { (\kappa+3)G_{\kappa+2}}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{\kappa+3}(n)
 &=\kappa+3-\frac{\kappa+4}{R_{\kappa+4}(n)}\\
 &=\kappa+3-\frac{(\kappa+3)G_{\kappa+2}}
 { (\kappa+2)G_{\kappa+1}}\\
 &=\frac{(\kappa+3)\bigl((\kappa+2)G_{\kappa+1}-G_{\kappa+2}\bigr)}
 { (\kappa+2)G_{\kappa+1}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By (1), the expression in parentheses is \((\kappa+1)G_\kappa\), proving (2).

Taking \(\kappa=0\) in (2) gives
\[
R_3(n)=\frac{3G_0}{2G_1}.
\]
Since \(F_0=0!+F_1=1+F_1\), we have
\[
G_0-G_1=(n-2)T(n).
\]
It follows that
\[
R_2(n)=2-\frac3{R_3(n)}
      =2-\frac{2G_1}{G_0}
      =\frac{2(n-2)T(n)}{G_0}. \tag{3}
\]
For \(n=3\), the same formula follows directly from the terminal value \(R_2(3)=2+3/4=11/4\). Thus (3) holds for every \(n\ge3\).

The expression \(G_0\) has a useful factorization. Since
\[
4(n-1)!=4(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)!,
\]
we obtain
\[
G_0=(n-2)D, \tag{4}
\]
where
\[
D=4(n-1)(n-3)!+T(n)F_0. \tag{5}
\]
Combining (3) and (4), one may already write
\[
R_2(n)=\frac{2T(n)}{D},
\]
but we will retain the factored form during the divisibility argument.

We now prove the main cancellation lemma.

**Lemma.** Suppose that \(p\) is prime, \(p>5\), and
\[
3\le n<p,\qquad n\ne6,\qquad p\mid T(n).
\]
Then the reduced numerator of \(R_2(n)\), and hence \(a(n)\), is \(p\).

Write
\[
T(n)=pm
\]
with \(m>0\). We first sharpen \(n<p\) to
\[
p\ge n+3. \tag{6}
\]
Certainly \(p\ge n+1\). If \(p=n+1\), then because
\[
T(n)=(n+1)^2-5,
\]
the divisibility \(p\mid T(n)\) would imply \(p\mid5\), contrary to \(p>5\). If \(p=n+2\), use
\[
T(n)=n(n+2)-4;
\]
then \(p\mid T(n)\) would imply \(p\mid4\), again impossible. This proves (6).

We also have \(n\ne4\). Indeed, \(T(4)=20\), and no prime greater than \(5\) divides \(20\).

Next we show
\[
m\le n-2. \tag{7}
\]
If instead \(m\ge n-1\), then (6) would give
\[
T(n)=pm\ge(n+3)(n-1)=n^2+2n-3=T(n)+1,
\]
a contradiction.

In fact,
\[
m\mid(n-3)!. \tag{8}
\]
To see this, consider any prime \(q\), and let \(q^e\) be the full \(q\)-power occurring in \(m\), with \(e>0\). Then \(q^e\mid m\), so by (7),
\[
2\le q^e\le n-2.
\]
We claim that equality \(q^e=n-2\) is impossible. If equality held, then \(n-2\mid m\), hence \(n-2\mid T(n)\). But from
\[
T(n)=(n-2)(n+4)+4
\]
we would obtain \(n-2\mid4\). Together with \(n\ge3\), this leaves only the small possibilities associated with divisors of \(4\). The possibility \(n=3\) is incompatible with \(q^e=n-2=1\); \(n=4\) was excluded; \(n=5\) gives \(3\nmid4\); and \(n=6\) is excluded by hypothesis. Thus \(q^e\ne n-2\), and therefore
\[
q^e\le n-3.
\]
Every positive integer at most \(n-3\), in particular \(q^e\), divides \((n-3)!\). This holds for the complete power of each prime in \(m\), so their product \(m\) divides \((n-3)!\), proving (8).

It follows from (5), (8), and \(T(n)=pm\) that
\[
m\mid D. \tag{9}
\]
We require the slightly stronger fact
\[
2m\mid D. \tag{10}
\]
For this, first note that when \(n\ge5\),
\[
F_0=0!+1!+2!+\cdots+(n-4)!

a
=1+1+2!+\cdots+(n-4)!
\]
is even: the first two terms sum to \(2\), and every later factorial is even.

We split according to the parity of \(n\).

If \(n\) is even, write \(n=2a\). Since \(n\ne4,6\) and \(n\ge3\), in this case \(n\ge8\). As one of \(a,a+1\) is even, write \(a(a+1)=2b\). Then
\[
T(n)=(2a+1)^2-5=4\bigl(a(a+1)-1\bigr)=4(2b-1), \tag{11}
\]
where \(2b-1\) is odd. Since \(p>5\) is odd and \(T(n)=pm\), equation (11) shows that \(4\mid m\); write
\[
m=4w.
\]
Moreover, \(w\) is odd, because (11) says that \(T(n)\) is divisible by \(4\) but not by \(8\), while \(p\) is odd.

Both terms of \(D\) are divisible by \(8\). Indeed, \((n-3)!\) is even, so
\[
8\mid4(n-1)(n-3)!,
\]
and (11), together with the evenness of \(F_0\), gives
\[
8\mid T(n)F_0.
\]
Thus \(8\mid D\). On the other hand, (9) and \(m=4w\) imply \(w\mid D\). Since \(w\) is odd, \(\gcd(8,w)=1\), and therefore
\[
8w=2m\mid D.
\]

If \(n\) is odd, then \((n+1)^2\) is divisible by \(4\), so
\[
T(n)=(n+1)^2-5
\]
is odd. Since \(p\) is odd, \(m=T(n)/p\) is odd as well. Also \(D\) is even. For \(n\ge5\), this follows because the first term in (5) is divisible by \(4\) and \(F_0\) is even. For the remaining odd case \(n=3\), direct substitution gives \(F_0=0\) and
\[
D=4(3-1)0!=8.
\]
Thus \(2\mid D\). Since \(m\mid D\) by (9) and \(m\) is odd, \(2\) and \(m\) are coprime, so \(2m\mid D\). This completes the proof of (10) in both parity cases.

We next prove that
\[
p\nmid D. \tag{12}
\]
Certainly \(p\mid T(n)F_0\). If also \(p\mid D\), equation (5) would imply
\[
p\mid4(n-1)(n-3)!.
\]
But \(p>5\), so \(p\nmid4\); also \(p>n\), so \(p\nmid n-1\), and no factor in \((n-3)!\) is divisible by \(p\). This is impossible, proving (12).

By (10), write
\[
D=2ms
\]
with \(s>0\). Equation (12) implies \(p\nmid s\), and since \(p\) is prime,
\[
\gcd(p,s)=1. \tag{13}
\]
Now use (3), (4), and \(T(n)=pm\):
\[
R_2(n)
 =\frac{2(n-2)T(n)}{G_0}
 =\frac{2(n-2)pm}{(n-2)D}
 =\frac{2(n-2)pm}{(n-2)2ms}
 =\frac ps.
\]
By (13), this last fraction is already in lowest terms. Its numerator is \(p\), so the reduced denominator of \(1/R_2(n)\) is \(p\). Thus \(a(n)=p\), proving the lemma.

It remains to construct an \(n\) satisfying the lemma for every prime in the required congruence classes.

Let \(p\) be prime and suppose
\[
p\equiv1\quad\hbox{or}\quad9\pmod {10}.
\]
Then \(p>5\), \(p\) is odd, and reduction modulo \(5\) gives
\[
p\equiv1\quad\hbox{or}\quad4\pmod5. \tag{14}
\]
The two nonzero numbers \(1\) and \(4\) are squares modulo \(5\). By quadratic reciprocity, because \(5\equiv1\pmod4\),
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right).
\]
Equation (14) makes the right-hand side equal to \(1\). Hence \(5\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\): there exists an integer \(x\), chosen with
\[
0\le x<p,
\]
such that
\[
x^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{15}
\]

First deal with \(p=11\). Taking \(n=3\), we have
\[
T(3)=3^2+2\cdot3-4=11.
\]
All hypotheses of the lemma hold, so \(a(3)=11\) (equivalently, directly, the continued fraction is \(1/(2-3/(-4))=4/11\)).

Now suppose \(p\ne11\). We show that the representative \(x\) in (15) satisfies \(x\ge4\). If \(x\) were \(0,1,2\), or \(3\), congruence (15) would force \(p\) to divide respectively \(5,4,1\), or \(4\), all impossible for \(p>5\). Thus \(x\ge4\).

Set
\[
n=x-1.
\]
Then \(n\ge3\), and since \(x<p\), also \(n<p\). Moreover,
\[
T(n)=(n+1)^2-5=x^2-5,
\]
so (15) gives
\[
p\mid T(n). \tag{16}
\]
The only remaining hypothesis of the lemma is \(n\ne6\). If \(n=6\), then \(x=7\), and (15) would imply
\[
p\mid 7^2-5=44=4\cdot11.
\]
As \(p>5\) is prime, this forces \(p=11\), contrary to the present assumption. Hence \(n\ne6\).

All hypotheses of the cancellation lemma now hold for this \(n=x-1\). Therefore \(a(n)=p\).

We have thus shown that every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) occurs as a reduced denominator in A363347.
